query:
We final-polish phenolic (Bakelite)-mounted, as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg on a Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher for quantitative SEM-EDS (5-15 kV). Until now the final step was 0.05 um colloidal silica for about 4-5 hours. When the puck came out of the bowl, the operator had to keep spraying the face with methanol, continuously, until it was cleaned, because colloidal silica left on the face starts drying, gelling and crystallizing within seconds of air exposure, bonds to the surface and is then very hard to remove; residual silica also adds Si to the EDS result. We are replacing colloidal silica with a water-based polycrystalline diamond suspension, 0.1 um (PACE Technologies DIAMAT WPC-0110: about 94-98% water, diamond, <=0.1% polyethylene glycol, <=0.2% surfactant; the vendor confirms no silica or alumina), on a low-nap synthetic polishing cloth with adhesive backing.
Questions:
(1) Does a 0.1 um water-based diamond suspension require the same keep-it-wet, continuous alcohol (methanol) spray handling when the specimen is removed, as colloidal silica does? Explain the mechanism that makes colloidal silica dry, gel and bond to a polished surface (sol-gel condensation, pH, Si-O-metal bonding, particle size and surface area) and whether a diamond suspension shares any of it. What residue, if any, does a dried water-based diamond suspension leave on aluminum (diamond particles, PEG or surfactant films), and how hard is it to remove compared with dried colloidal silica?
(2) What cleaning sequence after the final diamond step do the literature and manufacturers (Buehler, Struers, PACE, Allied, QATM/ATM) recommend for aluminum alloys: water rinse, detergent or soap, swabbing, ethanol or methanol or isopropanol rinse, ultrasonic time, drying with warm air or nitrogen? Is methanol specifically needed, or is ethanol or isopropanol equivalent?
(3) Does the water in the suspension, or a delay before cleaning, cause staining, pitting, hydroxide or oxide growth on Al-Si alloys that would change quantitative EDS (O, Al, Si, Mg), and how quickly?
Cite primary literature and manufacturer application notes where possible, and say clearly where evidence is missing.
task_summary: Assess Residue And Drying Behavior And Cleaning Protocols For Water Based 0.1μm Diamond Polishing On AlSi10Mg

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs

    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab

List of drug names to generate or filter results.

drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

    InterventionalAssignment:

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: paper_search

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Use the tools to answer the question: We final-polish phenolic (Bakelite)-mounted, as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg on a Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher for quantitative SEM-EDS (5-15 kV). Abstract:
Liquid metal reaction media provides exciting new avenues for synthesizing low‐dimensional materials. Here, the synthesis of atomically thin sheets and nanofibers of boehmite (γ‐AlOOH) and their transformation into cubic alumina (γ‐Al2O3) via annealing is explored. The sheets are as thin as one orthorhombic boehmite unit cell. The addition of aluminum into a room temperature alloy of gallium, followed by exposing the melt to either liquid water or water vapor, allows growing either 2D sheets or 1D fibers, respectively. The isolated oxide hydroxides feature large surface areas, with the sheet morphologies also showing a high Young's modulus. The method is green, since the liquid metal solvent can be fully reused. The ultrathin boehmite sheets are found suitable for the development of freestanding membrane filters that enable excellent separation of heavy metal ions and oil from aqueous solutions at extraordinary filtrate flux. The developed liquid metal‐based synthesis process offers a sustainable, green, and rapid method for synthesizing nanomorphologies of metal oxides which are challenging to obtain by conventional methods. The process is both sustainable and scalable and may be explored for the creation of other types of metal oxide compounds.

growing use of duplex stainless steels (DSSs) has spurred extensive research and development, particularly concerning weldability challenges. The increasing interest in additive manufacturing (AM) using directed energy deposition (DED) has further highlighted the need for precise sample preparation to ensure accurate microstructural characterization. This paper consolidates best practices for preparing samples to effectively reveal microstructures and secondary phases in DSSs. By optimizing polishing techniques and etching methods, the work provides guidelines for distinguishing ferrite and austenite across the base material, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and weld metal, while also enabling the detection of intermetallic phases and discrete secondary precipitates. Examples of typical deviations, etching phenomena, and potential pitfalls are also provided. The preparation strategies presented are tailored to support subsequent analysis using light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Azizur", title = "Synthesis and Microstructural Characterization of Ti/SiO2 Composite Powder Fabricated by Powder Metallurgy", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Jul", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10034168/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10034168/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Titanium/Silicon dioxide (Ti/SiO 2 ) composite powder was prepared through powder metallurgy process of high-energy mechanical mixing, uniaxial compaction under 200 MPa and vacuum sintering under 1100 °C for 4 h. Multi-technique characterization of phase composition, chemical bonding and microstructure was done by using the X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDX). XRD unambiguously confirmed retention of the α-quartz SiO 2 phase (ICDD 00-033-1161), with the principal (101) reflection at 2θ = 26.661° yielding d101 = 3.342 Å and hexagonal lattice parameters a = 4.913 Å, c = 5.405 Å. The crystallite size obtained from Scherrer analysis was 138 ± 10 nm, a nanoscale value corresponding to nanograin refinement. FTIR spectroscopy revealed the Si–O–Si asymmetric stretching band at 1010 cm -1 , the presence of surface silanol groups at 3512–3657 cm -1 , and the presence of Ti–O vibrational modes in the region of 528–663 cm -1 . Most importantly, the co-presence of Ti–O–Si mixed-bonding signatures yield spectroscopic evidence for chemical interaction at the Ti/SiO 2 interface, other than mechanical mixing. SEM/EDX analysis showed the distribution of elements and microstructural features of the composite, which was in agreement with the compositional targets. Thermodynamic stability of the composite is verified by the absence of secondary phases of TiSi₂ and TiO 2 in the XRD. These results provide a clear relationship between structure, processing, and properties of Ti/SiO 2 composites for applications such as aerospace, biomedical, and catalytic uses.

Abstract:
Abstract Silica nanoparticles (SNPs), one of the most widely researched materials in modern science, are now commonly exploited in surface coatings, biomedicine, catalysis, and engineering of novel self‐assembling materials. Theoretical approaches are invaluable to enhancing fundamental understanding of SNP properties and behavior. Tremendous research attention is dedicated to modeling silica structure, the silica‐water interface, and functionalization of silica surfaces for tailored applications. In this review, the range of theoretical methodologies are discussed that have been employed to model bare silica and functionalized silica. The evolution of silica modeling approaches is detailed, including classical, quantum mechanical, and hybrid methods and highlight in particular the last decade of theoretical simulation advances. It is started with discussing investigations of bare silica systems, focusing on the fundamental interactions at the silica‐water interface, following with a comprehensively review of the modeling studies that examine the interaction of silica with functional ligands, peptides, ions, surfactants, polymers, and carbonaceous species. The review is concluded with the perspective on existing challenges in the field and promising future directions that will further enhance the utility and importance of the theoretical approaches in guiding the rational design of SNPs for applications in engineering and biomedicine.

Abstract:
An attempt was made to control the surface charge of colloidal silica nanoparticles with 20 nm and 100 nm diameters. Untreated silica nanoparticles were determined to be highly negatively charged and have stable hydrodynamic sizes in a wide pH range. To change the surface to a positively charged form, various coating agents, such as amine containing molecules, multivalent metal cation, or amino acids, were used to treat the colloidal silica nanoparticles. Molecules with chelating amine sites were determined to have high affinity with the silica surface to make agglomerations or gel-like networks. Amino acid coatings resulted in relatively stable silica colloids with a modified surface charge. Three amino acid moiety coatings (L-serine, L-histidine, and L-arginine) exhibited surface charge modifying efficacy of L-histidine > L-arginine > L-serine and hydrodynamic size preservation efficacy of L-serine > L-arginine > L-histidine. The time dependent change in L-arginine coated colloidal silica was investigated by measuring the pattern of the backscattered light in a Turbiscan™. The results indicated that both the 20 nm and 100 nm L-arginine coated silica samples were fairly stable in terms of colloidal homogeneity, showing only slight coalescence and sedimentation.

Abstract:
Understanding the stability of chemical interactions at the polymer/metal oxide interface under humid conditions is vital to understand the long-term durability of hybrid systems. Therefore, the interface of ultrathin PMMA films on native aluminum oxide, deposited by reactive adsorption, was studied. The characterization of the interface of the coated substrates was performed using ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy in the Kretschmann geometry (ATR-FTIR Kretschmann) and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS). The formation of hydrogen bonds and carboxylate ionic bonds at the interface are observed. The formed ionic bond is stable up to 5 Torr water vapour pressure as shown by APXPS. However, when the coated samples are exposed to an excess of aqueous electrolyte, an increase in the amount of carboxylate bonds at the interface, as a result of hydrolysis of the methoxy group, is observed by ATR-FTIR Kretschmann. These observations, supported by ToF-SIMS spectra, lead to the proposal of an adsorption mechanism of PMMA on aluminum oxide, which shows the formation of methanol at the interface and the effect of water molecules on the different interfacial interactions.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) and post-CMP cleaning are critical steps in the current semiconductor manufacturing process. These processes require ensuring atomic-scale flatness and complete removal of contaminants. This review examines the use of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the atomic-scale mechanisms underlying CMP and postcleaning, focusing on four major MD methodologies: classical MD, reactive force field MD (ReaxFF), tight-binding quantum chemical MD (TB-QC MD), and ab initio MD (AIMD). Classical MD provides a foundation for simulating large-scale systems but lacks accuracy for modeling chemical reactions. ReaxFF allows real-time bond breaking and formation simulations during CMP. TB-QC MD combines quantum accuracy with classical efficiency, enabling exploration of the effects of chemical reactions on friction and material removal. AIMD directly calculates atomic interactions for precise depictions of chemical processes, although it is computationally expensive. MD simulations act as a “computational microscope”, enhancing CMP and postcleaning processes by quantifying interactions, material removal pathways, and contaminant desorption. Future research should address multiscale modeling challenges, improve AIMD efficiency, and develop accurate potential functions to propel semiconductor manufacturing toward greater precision and efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
The functional surfactants, as the additional additives in the standard glycol-based lubricant were studied and optimized to reduce and protect the surface of the magnetic read/write head from deposited contaminants during the lapping processes. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) results identified that the black contamination was bismuth (Bi) particles, came out from lapping plate during the lapping process due to wear. Selected surfactants exhibited the results in reduce and prevent the deposition of contaminants by forming the micelle beyond their critical micelle concentration (CMC) values. We found that both polyethoxylate alcohol (PEAL) and quaternary amines (QA) can form their micelle in glycol-based lubricant at the ratio of 1 %wt. Polyoxyethylene sorbitan monolaurate (PO) can protect the surface by its oxyethylene groups group at the 0.2 %wt in based lubricant. The characteristics and performances of modified lubricants were measured the change in magnetoresistive resistance value (%DMRR) from quasi-static test (QST). The modified lubricants had minor distribution failure of slider lower than standard lubricant. Moreover, the potentiodynamic polarization?measurement results indicated that additional surfactant can also yield almost 300% better performances than the standard lubricant in term of corrosion protection during lapping processes. Thus, these surfactants can function both as the contamination protective additive and as anti-corrosion additive. These modified lubricants can also keep the lap time and other physical performances to match the fabrication requirements.

The excerpt describes drying and gelation as a progressive sol-gel network-forming process. Water hydrolyzes alkoxy groups to produce silanol (Si-OH) groups; silanol condensation then creates siloxane (Si-O-Si) bonds while releasing water or alcohol. Continued condensation causes molecules and particles to aggregate into a continuous gel network. During drying, water and alcohol leave the network, causing shrinkage and reinforcing the gel. pH, water-to-silicon ratio, reagent concentration, temperature, ageing, and drying govern hydrolysis, condensation, particle formation, and final structure. At pH above 7, silica is more soluble and particles can grow; under specified alkaline conditions, spherical nanoparticles form, while higher temperatures produce larger particles. These factors imply that particle size and available surface area affect aggregation, network formation, drying shrinkage, and the extent of contact with a substrate. The excerpt documents strong adhesion of sol-gel films to silicon, silicon dioxide, and aluminum surfaces, but it does not explicitly describe Si-O-metal bond formation at polished metal surfaces. Thus, specific chemical bonding to metal, or a detailed role for surface area in metal adhesion, is not directly established in this passage; it only provides the broader silica condensation, particle-growth, drying, and adhesion framework.

The excerpt describes colloidal silica gelation as the formation of a three-dimensional network when condensed colloidal clusters crosslink and entrap the liquid. Silanol hydrolysis and subsequent silanol condensation/oxolation govern this process. At low pH, condensation is relatively slow and Si–O–Si chain growth, branching, and later crosslinking produce a polymeric, relatively low-pore-volume and microporous gel. Under basic conditions, hydrolyzed species are rapidly consumed, producing larger agglomerates that crosslink into a particulate gel with higher pore volume and mesoporosity. pH therefore controls both reaction rates and network architecture. During aging and drying, polycondensation creates additional chemical bonds, while syneresis expels liquid and causes shrinkage; coarsening can enlarge particle necks and fill smaller pores, reducing microporosity and surface area. The excerpt notes that silica’s partly covalent Si–O bonding permits flexible Si–O–Si angles and relatively open networks. It does not directly explain bonding to polished metal surfaces or explicitly discuss Si–O–metal bonds, particle-size optimization, or the detailed drying mechanism at a metal interface. It does, however, provide the relevant general framework: surface hydroxyl chemistry, condensation, colloidal-cluster size, pore structure, aging, and evolving surface area would be expected to influence adhesion and drying.

The hydrolysis rate has a minimum near pH 7, and pH, temperature, water-to-alkoxide ratio, and the organic substituent structure affect the process. The text also notes that silicate activation is pH-dependent and that acidification can convert silicate anions into tetrahedrally coordinated precursors capable of oxolation. Abstract:
This experimental work is aimed at studying the effect of microstructural modifications induced by post-processing heat treatments on the corrosion behavior of silicon-aluminum alloys produced by means of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The manufacturing technique leads to microstructures characterized by the presence of melt pools, which are quite different compared to casting alloys. In this study, the behavior of an AlSi10Mg alloy was evaluated by means of intergranular corrosion tests according to ISO 11846 standard on heat-treated samples ranging from 200 to 500 °C as well as on untreated samples. We found that temperatures above 200 °C reduced microhardness of the alloy, and different corrosion morphologies occurred due to the modification of both size and distribution of silicon precipitates. Selective penetrating attacks occurred at melt pool borders. The intergranular corrosion phenomena were less intense for as-produced specimens without heat treatments compared to the heat-treated specimens at 200 and 300 °C. General corrosion morphologies were noticed for specimens heat treated at temperatures exceeding 400 °C.

Abstract:
In this work, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) process was applied on AlSi10Mg samples, produced with laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), in the as printed condition and after different heat treatments, and, for comparison, on as-cast samples of AlSi10Mg. PEO process was performed in direct-current mode using high current densities and short time in a basic silicate electrolyte. For the first time, the effects of silicon morphology in L-PBF AlSi10Mg samples, in as printed condition and after different heat treatments, on the obtained PEO coating were investigated in terms of microstructure and corrosion properties. The microstructure of the substrate was characterized with optical and electron microscopy observations (optical microscopy OM, scanning electron microscopy SEM, and transmission electron microscopy TEM) and with X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis showed that heat treatments of annealing and solution treating modified the morphology and distribution of silicon in the samples obtained through L-PBF. The PEO coated samples were characterized with SEM, both on the surface and in the cross-section, and compositional analysis were performed with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis and elemental mapping. The coatings were also analyzed with XRD and the corrosion properties evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. Also microhardness tests were performed on the substrates and on the coatings. The microstructure of the coatings was strongly influenced by the silicon distribution. In particular, a non-uniform distribution of silicon and the presence of iron-rich intermetallic (obtained in the as-cast and solution treated samples) induced the formation of more porous and thinner coatings in comparison with the ones obtained in the as printed and annealed samples. The not-uniform silicon distribution produced a not-homogenous distribution of silicon into the coatings. The particular cellular structure of the as printed sample induced the formation of a coating with a higher amorphous fraction, in comparison with the ones produced on the other samples. The higher thickness and lower porosity of the coatings obtained on the annealed and as printed samples resulted in an increase of the corrosion resistance.

Abstract:
Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is a form of additive manufacturing that can directly make metal components and has begun to be employed in a variety of industrial situations. Moreover, the erosion characteristics of SLM-produced items have been documented relatively infrequently. In the current work, the erosion behavior of a heat-treated Al-Si-10% Mg alloy generated via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) has been investigated. The samples were printed in three directions (horizontal (0o), vertical (90o), and inclined (45o) on the build platform using the Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) system (EOS M 290) machine. Al%Si-10%Mg samples were given treatment (T5, T6). Optical and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) were used to examine the microstructure under both printed and heat-treated conditions. Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray Diffraction (XRD) were used to investigate the alloy's elemental composition and compound production. The erosion test was executed in each of the three orientations, plus heat-treated samples and as-printed samples. The selected input parameters were impingement angle and flow velocity. The erosion rate was examined and contrasted across orientations for printed and heat-treated conditions to establish the best orientation. The post-eroded surface was analysed using SEM, EDS, and XRD to evaluate possible erosion processes. The key findings were: T5 heat-treated samples sustain well and have the least mass loss; Horizontal (0°) oriented samples undergo less erosion compared to other orientations; T6 heat-treated samples show maximum erosion on printed samples, and hence it is not recommended. T5 heat treatment is proven to be superior in providing high erosion resistance, followed by printed and T6 heat-treatment, respectively. The heat treatment effects are more significant than the orientation effects in determining the erosion resistance of the Al10SiMg alloy. The erosion mechanisms, such as ploughing, melting, and cratering, were identified.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) shows potential in metal additive manufacturing for producing complex components. However, achieving ideal hardness and minimizing porosity poses a significant challenge. This study explores the impact of part orientation, scanning methods, and hatching distance on the hardness and porosity of AlSi10Mg alloy produced through L-PBF. Utilizing a Box–Behnken design of experiments (DOE), cubic samples were systematically produced. Hardness was quantitatively assessed using Vickers hardness tests, while porosity measurements involved 2D image analysis of polished scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples, the porosity percentages analyzed using ImageJ software. The results demonstrate that both scanning strategy and hatching distance significantly influence hardness and porosity. The spiral scanning pattern notably enhances hardness and reduces porosity. In contrast, the bidirectional scanning strategy results in lower hardness and more pronounced porosity formations. An inverse correlation between grain size distribution and hardness was observed, with finer grain sizes leading to higher hardness values, indicating that grain refinement improves mechanical properties. Additionally, a negative relationship between hardness and porosity was established, emphasizing the importance of minimizing porosity to enhance material hardness. These findings contribute to the overall understanding of the L-PBF additive manufacturing process, providing valuable insights for optimizing material properties and ensuring the mechanical integrity of high-performance L-PBF produced metal parts.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) revolutionary technologies open new opportunities and challenges. They allow low-cost manufacturing of parts with complex geometries and short time-to-market of products that can be exclusively customized. Additive manufactured parts often need post-printing surface modification. This study aims to review novel environmental-friendly surface finishing process of 3D-printed AlSi10Mg parts by electroless deposition of gold, silver, and gold–silver alloy (e.g., electrum) and to propose a full process methodology suitable for effective metallization. This deposition technique is simple and low cost method, allowing the metallization of both conductive and insulating materials. The AlSi10Mg parts were produced by the additive manufacturing laser powder bed fusion (AM-LPBF) process. Gold, silver, and their alloys were chosen as coatings due to their esthetic appearance, good corrosion resistance, and excellent electrical and thermal conductivity. The metals were deposited on 3D-printed disk-shaped specimens at 80 and 90 °C using a dedicated surface activation method where special functionalization of the printed AlSi10Mg was performed to assure a uniform catalytic surface yielding a good adhesion of the deposited metal to the substrate. Various methods were used to examine the coating quality, including light microscopy, optical profilometry, XRD, X-ray fluorescence, SEM–energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM, and XPS analyses. The results indicate that the developed coatings yield satisfactory quality, and the suggested surface finishing process can be used for many AM products and applications.

Abstract:
Laser Powder Bed Fusion is the most attractive additive manufacturing technology for its capability to produce metal components with complex geometry. One of the main drawbacks is the poor surface roughness. In this work, different scan strategies and process parameters were studied and their effect on surface roughness, alloy microstructure, and metallurgical defects were discussed. The results highlighted that only tailored process conditions could combine acceptable roughness and absence of metallurgical defects. For the upskin, it has been seen that, although by increasing the Volumetric Energy Density value the Ra decreases, Volumetric Energy Density values higher than 69 J/mm3 determine meltpool instability with consequent formation of gas defects in the subsurface area. Similarly, by increasing the Linear Energy Density value, the Ra of the lateral surfaces decreases, but above 0.37 J/mm, metallurgical defects form in the subsurface area. This study also highlighted that the proposed process involves only a contained increase of the production times. In fact, the evaluation of the increased production times, related to the adoption of this multi-scanning strategy, is of fundamental importance to consider if the proposed process can be advantageously applied on an industrial scale.

Abstract:
This paper presents a new production method for a spherical and monocrystalline aluminum powder. Aluminum powder of irregular particle shapes was mixed with silica nanoparticles and heated to a temperature above the melting point of aluminum. Due to its molten state, high surface tension, and poor wettability, the aluminum particles were transformed into liquid and spherical droplets separated by silica nanoparticles. The spherical shape was then retained when the aluminum particles solidified. The influence of the processing temperature on the particle shape, phase composition, and microstructure was investigated. Moreover, calorimetric, X-ray diffraction, grain size, and scanning electron microscopy with electron backscatter diffraction (SEM-EBSD) measurements of the particles’ microstructure are presented. It is proven that, by this means, a spherical and monocrystalline aluminum powder can be efficiently created directly from an air-atomized irregular powder. The observed phenomenon of particles becoming round is of great importance, especially when considering powder preparation for powder-based additive manufacturing processes.

The excerpt recommends prompt, gentle removal of polishing residues after colloidal-silica or other polishing steps. The stated cleaning sequence begins with rinsing under running water using dishwashing soap, accompanied by gentle rubbing with fine tissue or cotton; firm manual cleaning should be avoided because it can scratch the surface. If colloidal-silica residue remains, the sample may be rinsed with cold water and gently wiped using soft cotton moistened with ethanol. Hot water should be avoided because it can crystallize silica and require repolishing. Deionized water is preferred after etching or where image quality is important, since tap water may leave contamination. A final ethanol rinse prevents water stains, after which the sample should be dried immediately with warm air or clean compressed air. The surface should not be wiped with tissue or cloth after final cleaning, to avoid reintroducing fibers or static charge. Ultrasonic cleaning is described as highly effective before SEM analysis and useful for removing residual silica, particularly between preparation stages. Abstract:
The functionalization of fine primary particles by atomic layer deposition (particle ALD) provides for nearly perfect nanothick films to be deposited conformally on both external and internal particle surfaces, including nanoparticle surfaces. Film thickness is easily controlled from several angstroms to nanometers by the number of self-limiting surface reactions that are carried out sequentially. Films can be continuous or semi-continuous. This review starts with a short early history of particle ALD. The discussion includes agitated reactor processing, both atomic and molecular layer deposition (MLD), coating of both inorganic and polymer particles, nanoparticles, and nanotubes. A number of applications are presented, and a path forward, including likely near-term commercial products, is given.

Abstract:
Abstract Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in electron microscopy has been widely used in many research areas since it provides precise information on the chemical composition of subcellular structures that may be correlated with their high resolution images. In EDS the characteristic X-rays typical of each element are analyzed and the new detectors - an example of which we describe - allow for setting precisely the area of measurements and acquiring signals as a point analysis, as a linescan or in the image format of the desired area. Mapping of the elements requires stringent methods of sample preparation to prevent redistribution/loss of the elements as well as elimination of the risk of overlapping spectra. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses may be performed at a low probe current suitable for thin biological samples. Descriptions of preparation techniques, drawbacks and precautions necessary to obtain reliable results are provided, including data on standards, effects of specimen roughness and quantification. Data on EPMA application in different fields of biomedical and agricultural studies are reviewed. In this review we refer to recent EDS/EPMA applications in medical diagnostics, studies on air pollution and agrochemicals as well as on plant models used to monitor the environment.

The article reports that aluminum oxidized in dry air at room temperature for 5 hours develops an oxide approximately 15 Å thick; a separate measurement gives 14 Å after 1 hour in dry oxygen at room temperature. Exposure to humid conditions causes adsorbed water to hydrate the oxide, producing Al(OH)3 and increasing the measured oxide thickness. For pure aluminum preoxidized in dry oxygen, the thickness increases from about 15–16 Å to 22 Å after one week at 80% relative humidity. The hydration-related increase is effectively complete after one week: exposure for up to one month produces no further measured increase. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative correction or detailed assessment of EDS oxygen, aluminum, silicon, and magnesium concentrations. It reports that EDX detected only aluminum in the matrix, while a white surface spot contained aluminum, silicon, and iron; subsequent surface analysis found silicon in the oxide layer and iron beneath the surface. ## pqac-00000018

From text 'galvin2001imagingofsurface pages 9-11'.

S. P. Galvin, B. J. Griffin, and J. Browne. Imaging of surface strain and polishing artefacts in fused silica by environmental scanning electron microscopy. Journal of Materials Science, 36:5683-5696, Dec 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1012586204236, doi:10.1023/a:1012586204236. This article has 10 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides direct evidence that polishing abrasive particles can retain a thin silica-containing overlayer after polishing and adhesion to a specimen surface. Chemically adhered ceria particles on fused silica displayed contrast attributed to a thin silica overlayer, demonstrating that the apparent surface composition can reflect contamination or deposited material rather than the underlying substrate. Charge-contrast imaging (CCI) was sensitive to this thin deposit and could also reveal linear strain defects beneath an adhered ceria layer approximately 300 nm thick. The authors compared CCI observations with backscattered-electron images and confirmed the silica overlayer independently using transmission electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (TEM-EDS). This supports the interpretation that polishing residues may produce a silicon signal in surface-sensitive analytical measurements and potentially bias EDS-based composition, especially where the contaminant forms a continuous or localized film over the polished surface. The excerpt does not provide quantitative EDS error values, detection limits, or a direct calibration for colloidal silica residue on metallographic specimens, but it establishes the mechanism and analytical risk: a thin silica deposit can obscure or alter measurements of the underlying material.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 23-25'.

Elin Marianne Westin, Jan Yngve Jonsson, Kaue Correa Riffel, Martijn Marinus Bos, Constantinos Goulas, and Antonio José Ramirez. Enhancing microstructural analysis: best practices for preparing duplex stainless steel welds and additive manufacturing deposits. Welding in the World, 70:4549-4581, Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x, doi:10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies polishing and cleaning artifacts that can compromise metallographic interpretation and potentially affect EDS microanalysis. Excessive grinding or polishing force may embed residue in the specimen surface, especially in softer austenitic regions, and can produce smearing or deformation. Insufficient lubrication increases drag and worsens this contamination. The text also emphasizes that polishing plates and cloths must be cleaned properly to prevent cross-contamination between specimens. Ultrasonic cleaning with ethanol or isopropanol is recommended as a beneficial cleaning step. The excerpt specifically reports that SEM/EDS confirmed preparation residues in an apparently defective region, demonstrating that residues can be mistaken for microstructural constituents. In mounted specimens, SiO2 polishing material can enter crevices between the specimen and mounting material and continue etching if it is not adequately removed before embedding or during subsequent cleaning. Although the passage does not specifically quantify silicon contamination from colloidal silica in EDS, it directly supports the conclusion that silica-containing polishing residues and other preparation contaminants may remain on or enter the specimen surface and should be removed before quantitative analysis. Surface condition, cleaning, and verification by SEM/EDS are therefore important when anomalous silicon signals or apparent inclusions are observed.

Metallurgical and Materials Transactions A, 53:345-358, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-021-06474-4, doi:10.1007/s11661-021-06474-4. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt describes metallographic preparation and EDS characterization of stainless-steel powder samples. Cross-sections were mounted in conductive Bakelite, ground, and polished to a 0.05 µm non-crystallizing SiO2 suspension finish. The prepared samples were examined by SEM with secondary-electron or backscattered-electron imaging, and elemental composition was measured by EDS. Analyses used Zeiss Sigma FEG-SEM or Versa 3D SEM systems operating at 10 kV, equipped with silicon-drift detectors and processed with AztecFeature OI software. This preparation detail is relevant to investigating colloidal-silica residue because the final polishing step explicitly introduces SiO2 immediately before EDS measurement, creating a potential source of surface silicon if the specimen is inadequately cleaned. However, the excerpt does not report whether polishing residue remained, whether silicon was detected as an artifact, or whether quantitative EDS results were corrected for such contamination. It therefore supports identifying the polishing compound as a possible contamination source and documenting the analytical conditions, but does not provide experimental evidence about residue effects on quantitative microanalysis.

Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports the conclusion that polishing can alter the near-surface physical and chemical composition of metallographic specimens, potentially affecting quantitative EDS results. Colloidal silica is identified as a mechanical-chemical polishing method, and its use can produce a surface condition distinct from that produced by diamond-only mechanical polishing. The authors emphasize that abrasive wear modifies surface properties and that finely polished materials may retain an amorphous surface compound and subsurface lattice disorder. They also note that surface contamination or reaction products may be introduced indirectly by a polishing disc contaminated with wear debris from the current or a previous polishing operation. Such debris could plausibly include residues from the polishing compound, although this excerpt does not specifically identify silicon contamination or measure a Si EDS artifact caused by colloidal silica. The passage further indicates that surface reaction products can form through diffusion involving residual water and can continue modifying surface composition during storage. Therefore, the excerpt is relevant as general evidence that polishing residues, transferred debris, amorphous layers, and post-polishing surface reactions can influence EDS quantitative microanalysis, but it does not provide direct experimental confirmation of colloidal-silica-derived silicon contamination.

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 14-15'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is relevant to polishing-related surface contamination and its effect on quantitative electron-probe or EDS-style microanalysis, although it does not specifically identify colloidal silica. It emphasizes that polishing can produce a surface layer or altered surface composition, causing quantitative analytical results to differ from the true bulk composition. In the example, a diamond-polished chalcopyrite specimen was compared with one receiving a final soft-pad polish using chromic oxide dispersed in water; the resulting EPMA concentrations demonstrated sensitivity to the polishing procedure. The authors recommend preparing both unknown specimens and reference materials with exactly the same polishing procedure to minimize matrix and surface-composition differences. They also note that surface composition can change during prolonged storage in air, so analyses should be conducted immediately after polishing. Measurements at different electron-beam energies produced substantially different Ag concentrations (0.85% at 8 keV versus 0.3% at 15 keV), indicating nonuniform composition with depth. This supports the interpretation that polishing residues or polishing-induced altered layers can generate contamination artifacts, particularly at low beam energies that sample nearer the surface. For colloidal silica specifically, the excerpt provides general methodological support but no direct discussion of silica residue, silicon peaks, or cleaning/removal procedures.

1.4  PREPARATION METHODS FOR IRON-BASED ALLOYS

1.4.1  THE ‘‘TRADITIONAL’’ METHOD

Over the past 40 years, a general procedure has evolved that is quite successful for pre-
paring most iron and steel alloys. This method is based on grinding with silicon carbide
waterproof papers through a series of grits, then rough polishing with one or more diamond
abrasive sizes, followed by fine polishing with one or more alumina suspensions of different
particle size. This procedure will be called the ‘‘traditional’’ method, and is described in
Table 1.4, listing equivalent ANSI/CAMI and FEPA grit sizes for the SiC paper.

the force applied to a specimen would not be very consistent. Complementary motion means

manual preparation (in manual polishing, the metallographer rotates the specimen in the
direct opposite to the platen rotation, that is, contra rotation). Some machines can be set

‘‘traditional’’ approach when automated. The traditional method is not rigid, however, as

Ultra-Prep diamond disks, the Ultra-Plan stainless steel mesh cloth (diamond is applied
during use), the BuehlerHercules H and S rigid grinding disks (RGD) (diamond is applied
during use), or lapping platens of several types (diamond is applied and becomes embedded
in the surface during use). With this huge array of products to choose from, how can the
metallographer decide what to use? Each of these products has advantages and  dis-
advantages, and this is only the first step.
   One or more steps using diamond abrasives on napless surfaces usually follow planar
grinding. PSA-backed silk, nylon, or polyester cloths are widely used. These give good cut-
ting rates, maintain flatness, and minimize relief. Silk cloths, such as the Ultra-PolTM cloth,
provide the best flatness and excellent surface finishes relative to the diamond size used.
Ultra-PadTM cloth, a thicker hard, woven cloth, is more aggressive, gives nearly as good a
surface finish, similar excellent flatness, and longer life than an Ultra-Pol cloth. Synthetic
chemotextile pads, such as the Texmet  1000 and 2000 cloths, give excellent flatness and are
more aggressive than silk. They are excellent for retaining second-phase particles and inclu-
sions. Diamond suspensions are most popular with automated polishers as they can be added
easily during polishing; although it is still best to charge the cloth initially with diamond paste
of the same size to get polishing started quickly. Final polishing could be performed with a
very fine diamond size, such as 0.1 mm diamond, depending upon the material, your needs,
and personal preferences

1.3.5.4  Polishing Abrasives

Polishing usually involves the use of one or more of the following abrasives: diamond,
aluminum oxide (Al2O3), and amorphous silicon dioxide (SiO2) in colloidal suspension.
Diamond abrasives were introduced to metallographers commercially in the late 1940s.
However, their use in metallography goes back to at least the late 1920s. Diamond abrasives
were first introduced in a carrier paste but later aerosol and slurry forms were introduced.
Virgin natural diamond was used initially, and is still available in Metadi  diamond paste.
Later, synthetic diamond was introduced, first of the monocrystalline form, similar in mor-
phology to natural diamond, and then in polycrystalline form. Metadi II diamond paste uses
monocrystalline synthetic diamond. Metadi diamond suspension uses natural diamond, while
Metadi Supreme suspensions use polycrystalline diamond. Figure 1.32 illustrates the general
shape of synthetic monocrystalline and polycrystalline diamond. Synthetic monocrystal-
line diamond looks much like natural (monocrystalline) diamond. Studies have shown that
cutting rates are higher for many materials using polycrystalline diamond compared to
monocrystalline diamond.
   Alumina has been used for many years and is made by the calcinations process [9] starting
from alum. The final particle shape and size is controlled to produce alpha and gamma
alumina. Alpha alumina has an anhedral (allotriomorphic) shape with a 2:1 aspect ratio and
no obvious sharp cutting edges. Alpha alumina has a hexagonal crystal structure and is
slightly harder than gamma alumina with a cubic crystal structure. The powder is mixed with
distilled water to form a slurry. Although the mean particle size of alpha alumina is 0.3 mm,
and the mean size of gamma alumina is 0.05 mm, it is common to see agglomerated particles
that act larger. Deagglomerated alumina powders and slurries [10] are more free of this
problem, but not totally free of agglomerates. A new type of alumina, made from the seeded
gel process, has been introduced and is called MasterprepTM alumina with a mean particle
size of 0.05 mm. Its polishing action is quite different to traditional alumina.
    Colloidal silica consists of spherical particles of amorphous silica, Figure 1.33, suspended
in a basic colloid with a pH of typically 9.5 to 10 (the possible range is broader, but this is
the range widely used for metallographic polishing [2,11,12]). The mean particle size  is
generally in the range of 0.2 to 0.6 mm. Freezing causes the particles to precipitate and
crystallize and destroys the solution. Evaporation does the same. Additives are frequently
used to retard evaporation and freezing. The colloid does contain ions, typically of sodium.
The polishing action comes from chemo-mechanical action, much like an attack polish.

   The writer started using colloidal silica for final polishing steel specimens in 1974, after
learning about their use in the electronics industry for final polishing of silicon single-crystal
wafers. Colloidal silica has a low removal rate but is very effective at removing the last
remaining damage in the preparation cycle. But, it is not without its problems. One must
carefully wash off the polishing cloth after use to prevent crystalline silica from forming when
it dries. If this happens, the polishing cloth will scratch the next specimens being prepared.
It is very hard to remove the crystalline silica from such a cloth. Specimens are more difficult
to clean after polishing, as a thin white layer of the polishing solution will adhere to the
surface. Scrubbing with cotton soaked in a detergent solution will eventually remove it. But,
to make removal easy, particularly when using an automated polishing machine, stop adding
abrasive with about 15 to 20 sec remaining in the polishing period. With about 10 sec
remaining, direct a water jet onto the cloth. The water will wash the cloth and the specimen.
When the wheel stops, simply remove the specimen holder, rinse the specimens under
running water, squirt ethanol onto the specimen surfaces to displace the water, and blow it
dry under hot air. With this method, it is usually unnecessary to even scrub the specimen
surfaces with cotton and a liquid detergent before rinsing.



1.3.6  PREPARATION PROCEDURES

The increased use of automated polishing devices has fostered the adoption of more
efficient, better preparation procedures designed to reveal the true structure (specimen
integrity  concept).  If an automated  system  is  used  with  a  specimen  holder  that
accommodates a number of specimens (number varies with size and format,  i.e., 8 or
12 inch wheel size (200 or 300 mm)), mounted or unmounted, and if the pressure is applied
centrally, then the first step of grinding must remove the damage introduced by sectioning
and make all of the specimens co-planar. This step is often called planar grinding. If the
force  is applied to each specimen individually (only practical with mounted specimens),
then the first step of grinding is used to remove sectioning damage as the specimens areFerrous Metallography                                                            33


not rigidly constrained in the holder. The application of force to each individual specimen
seats each specimen independently of the others. In grinding or polishing, the head can
rotate in either the same direction as the platen (complementary) or in the opposite
direction to the platen (contra). Contra rotation is more aggressive than complementary
rotation producing a higher removal rate but this does not always produce better results.
Complementary rotation is safest to use. For final polishing, contra rotation is helpful in
that the polishing slurry is not swept off the surface as readily as with complementary
rotation.
   Numerous surfaces can be used for the rough grinding or planar grinding step depend-
ing upon the equipment available and the nature of the work. For planar grinding, a high-
speed grinder using a coarse grit aluminum oxide stone has been commonly used. This
produces fast, efficient removal of sectioning damage. However, it does require purchase of
an expensive single-purpose machine. Grinding stones are expensive, their surface must be
treated with a diamond tool before each use, and the stone does create a significant depth of
damage.
    If the specimen has been cut using the proper abrasive wheel, then the depth of damage
and the roughness of the cut are substantially less than from band sawing or power hack
sawing. In such a case, a relatively fine abrasive can be employed to remove the section-
ing damage. Going to a stone is going backwards, that  is, to a much coarser grit than
needed. Wafering blades or thin abrasive cutoff wheels produce even less damage than a
standard abrasive wheel. If the grinding/polishing machine has individual force ability,
then the starting grinding surface can be equivalent to 240 or 320 grit SiC paper.
   Obviously, ordinary SiC abrasive paper (waterproof) can be used for the first grind-
ing step. Other surfaces are also possible, for example, lapping platens, rigid grinding di

Question: What is the difference between metalbonded and resin-
bonded ULTRA-PREP Discs, especially regarding their use?

Answer: The metal bonding is done with an electrolytic nickel
plating which holds the particles firmly in place. The resin bond,
being polymeric, holds the particles much like a layer of glue. The
metalbonding is more rigid and makes the disc most suitable for
grinding harder materials. When soft metals are ground with the
metal-bonded disc, seizing may occur between the nickel plating
and certain soft metals, such as aluminum. Instead of cutting the
aluminum, seizing leads to adhesion of aluminum to the disc and
tearing of the aluminum surface. Resin bonding does not cause
seizing and prevents this problem. Resin-bonded discs can grind very
hard metals also but they will not last as long as a metal-bonded disc
and they will probably exhibit a lower removal rate. Resin-bonded
discs will produce a smoother surface finish than nickel-bonded
discs for the same particle size.

Abstract:

 This study aimed to determine the effect of surface metallographic preparation (grinding, diamond polishing, and chemo-mechanical polishing using silica and hydrogen peroxide) on the surface roughness, morphology, chemical composition, and electrochemical behaviour of Ti-6Al-4V alloy. Roughness decreases from ca. 0.2 m to 0.02 m from grinding to polishing. A typical + microstructure can be observed only after chemo-mechanical polishing. The average composition of ca. 6 wt.% Al, 4 wt.% V, and rest Ti was determined regardless of the surface preparation. X-ray phtotoelectron spectroscopy revealed that the thickness of the oxide layer formed on chemo-mechanical polished samples is half that of ground samples. The metallographic preparation largely affects the corrosion behaviour of Ti-6Al-4V, which was investigated using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarisation in 0.9 wt.% NaCl and artificial saliva at 37C. At the open circuit potential, the chemo-mechanically polished Ti-6Al-4 samples showed superior corrosion resistance over ground samples. At potentials over 2.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl, increased current densities were noted for chemo-mechanically polished samples, presumably related to the oxidation to a thicker oxide.
