## pqac-00000035

From text 'westin2025enhancingmicrostructuralanalysis pages 9-10'.

Elin Marianne Westin, Jan Yngve Jonsson, Kaue Correa Riffel, Martijn Marinus Bos, Constantinos Goulas, and Antonio José Ramirez. Enhancing microstructural analysis: best practices for preparing duplex stainless steel welds and additive manufacturing deposits. Welding in the World, 70:4549-4581, Dec 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x, doi:10.1007/s40194-025-02286-x. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not specifically characterize residue from diamond polishing suspensions, establish whether diamond is chemically inert toward metals, describe diamond–metal bonding, or discuss PEG/surfactant films or the need for an immediate alcohol spray after diamond polishing. Its directly relevant comparison concerns colloidal silica (SiO2) and alumina residues. Residual SiO2 may remain on the surface as streaks or a white haze, especially over ferrite, obscuring phase contrast and potentially affecting subsequent etching or imaging. The recommended approach is to use water during the final 30 seconds of polishing to remove residual SiO2, then rinse promptly; persistent residue can be removed with cold water and gentle wiping using ethanol-moistened soft cotton. Hot water should be avoided because it may crystallize silica and require repolishing. For final cleaning, deionized water is preferred after etching, followed by an ethanol rinse and immediate drying with warm air or clean compressed air. The excerpt also notes that residual colloidal alumina particles can embed in the surface and locally alter contrast if not fully removed. Thus, the passage supports general residue-removal and cleaning practices, but it provides no evidence for the specific chemical or film-forming behavior of diamond suspensions.

Abstract:
The process of cutting, mechanical and chemical treatment of the undoped and doped ZnSe crystal surface has been studied. The chemical interaction of zinc selenide surface with bromine emerging solutions of H2O2 – HBr and H2O2 – HBr – organic solvent has been studied. The surface states after chemical etching have been investigated using electron, metallographic and atomic force microscopy, and it was shown that the surface state is improved after chemical etching. Etchant selection to develop slow polishing compositions for chemical-mechanical polishing of investigated materials has been made. Efficient methods for washing samples solutions have been developed after different types of ZnSe surface treatment: cutting of the crystal, mechanical surface treatment, chemical removing the surface damaged layer.

Abstract:
In this study, QuEChERS extraction was combined with dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction (DLLME) to extract pesticides from tropical fruits for determination by a highly accurate and sensitive liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF-MS/MS) system. The QuEChERS method served as a matrix clean-up tool and the DLLME method preconcentrated the analytes for their determination at trace levels. All parameter variables of the DLLME method were optimized to improve the extraction output and lower the limits of detection and quantification (LOD and LOQ) for all the analytes. Under the optimum experimental conditions, the LOD and LOQ values were found in the range of 0.004–0.013 and 0.27–0.61 μg l−1, respectively. The detection limits achieved by direct LC-QTOF-MS/MS analysis were increased by about 10–260 folds using the optimized DLLME method. To assess the accuracy and applicability of the developed method, spike recovery experiments on tropical fruits were carried out. The matrix matching calibration method was used to enhance the quantification accuracy of the analytes in kiwi, pineapple, and mango matrices, with percent recoveries ranging between 89 and 117%.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'galvin2001imagingofsurface pages 9-11'.

S. P. Galvin, B. J. Griffin, and J. Browne. Imaging of surface strain and polishing artefacts in fused silica by environmental scanning electron microscopy. Journal of Materials Science, 36:5683-5696, Dec 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1012586204236, doi:10.1023/a:1012586204236. This article has 10 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides evidence that polishing-related particulate contamination and thin silica-containing overlayers can remain on fused-silica surfaces and affect electron imaging and elemental analysis. In particular, adhered ceria particles were covered by a thin silica overlayer, inferred from their imaging contrast and independently confirmed by TEM-EDS after particles were scraped from the surface. This supports the general possibility that polishing or preparation can leave silicon-bearing residue on a surface and that the residue may be associated with abrasive particles or surface films. However, the passage does not specifically study colloidal silica polishing, quantify silicon residue by surface-sensitive XPS, compare cleaned versus uncleaned specimens, or prescribe a cleaning procedure. It also reports that SEM-EDS found identical chemical compositions in deformed and undeformed regions, but this comparison concerns silica deformation rather than proving the absence of a thin polishing residue. The excerpt therefore supports caution when interpreting EDS or other surface analyses after polishing: a thin silica overlayer may mask or alter the apparent composition of adhered material. It does not establish whether routine cleaning removes colloidal-silica residue or what cleaning method is effective.


---

## pqac-00000037

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 19-21'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is relevant to the possibility that metallographic preparation alters the surface chemistry measured by XPS or EDS, but it does not specifically report silicon contamination from colloidal silica or provide a cleaning procedure for removing silica residue. It states that polishing with colloidal silica can reveal grain structure and that abrasive wear modifies the physical and chemical properties of the polished surface. More generally, the authors emphasize that quantitative x-ray results can vary with polishing materials, equipment, and experimental parameters, even after an optically polished surface has been obtained. The discussion also notes that polishing can produce an amorphous surface compound and subsurface lattice disorder, with damage generally lower after CMP than after purely mechanical polishing with diamond abrasives. Surface reaction products may form through contact with contaminated polishing surfaces or polishing-disc wear debris, and the surface composition can continue changing during storage. These points support treating colloidal-silica-polished specimens as potentially chemically modified and recognizing that residues or reaction products may affect surface-sensitive analysis. However, the supplied pages do not identify a silicon signal, quantify silica deposition, compare XPS/EDS results before and after cleaning, or recommend a specific cleaning method. Evidence for those specific claims would need to come from other sections or sources.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 14-15'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports the general conclusion that metallographic preparation can alter the measured near-surface composition and therefore affect quantitative elemental analysis. It describes a comparison between diamond polishing and a final soft-pad polish using chromic oxide dispersed in water; the resulting EPMA data were sensitive to surface composition. The authors recommend that specimens and reference materials be prepared rigorously using the same polishing procedure to minimize differences caused by preparation. They also caution that surface composition may change during prolonged storage in air, so analyses should be performed immediately after polishing. These observations are relevant to assessing possible colloidal-silica residue: a polishing medium left on or incorporated into the surface could produce an apparent silicon signal in surface-sensitive XPS and potentially affect shallow-volume EDS measurements. However, this excerpt does not specifically identify colloidal silica, report silicon contamination from silica polishing, or describe a cleaning procedure for removing such residue. It therefore provides general evidence for polishing-related surface contamination and analytical bias, but not direct experimental confirmation or a prescribed cleaning method for silica residues.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'taborelli2020cleaningandsurface pages 8-10'.

Mauro Taborelli. Cleaning and surface properties. Preprint, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.01585, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2006.01585. This article has 48 citations.

The excerpt does not directly discuss metallographic preparation with colloidal silica, silica residue, or EDS detection of polishing-derived silicon. It does, however, provide relevant general guidance for interpreting and removing surface contamination before elemental analysis. XPS is described as a highly surface-sensitive technique, probing approximately the upper 1–3 nm and detecting most elements at levels near 1 atomic%, so a thin silicon-containing residue left by colloidal silica polishing could plausibly affect XPS results even if it is not obvious macroscopically. The text emphasizes that cleanliness assessment should be matched to the application and that analytical methods identify contaminants rather than necessarily proving functional cleanliness. Ion or glow-discharge cleaning can remove topmost contaminants and, at sufficiently high dose, native oxide; argon is chemically nonreactive but may implant into the surface, while oxygen-containing gas mixtures are effective for eliminating carbon. These treatments should therefore be used cautiously when silicon or oxide chemistry is being measured, because sputtering can modify the surface composition. Ozone/UV cleaning is presented mainly for hydrocarbon contamination and may oxidize copper or aluminium, but no evidence is given that it removes particulate or chemically bonded silica residue. The excerpt offers no specific protocol for colloidal-silica removal; wet cleaning, rinsing, or validation on a control sample would need to be established from other sources.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'balart2022automatedsemedsanalysis pages 6-6'.

MarÍa J. Balart, Xinjiang Hao, and Claire L. Davis. Automated sem/eds analysis for assessment of trace cross-contamination in 316l stainless steel powders. Metallurgical and Materials Transactions A, 53:345-358, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-021-06474-4, doi:10.1007/s11661-021-06474-4. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt documents metallographic preparation involving grinding and polishing with a 0.05 µm non-crystallizing SiO2 suspension, followed by SEM imaging and EDS analysis. It therefore establishes that colloidal or non-crystallizing silica polishing was used before elemental analysis of the samples. However, this passage does not report whether polishing left detectable silicon or silica residue on the surface, whether such residue interfered with EDS or XPS measurements, or whether a cleaning procedure was applied to remove it. It also does not mention XPS analysis. The excerpt describes analytical instrumentation and software, including SEM-EDS systems with silicon drift detectors, but provides no comparison between cleaned and uncleaned surfaces and no quantitative assessment of polishing-related contamination. Thus, it offers methodological context relevant to investigating silica residue, but no direct evidence about residue persistence, its analytical impact, or effective cleaning methods.

Abstract:
This article presents a review of the current research into the diamond retention capacity of metal matrices, which largely determines the service life and working performance of diamond tools. The constitution of diamond retention capacity, including physical adsorption force, mechanical inlaying force, and chemical bonding force, are described. Improved techniques are summarized as three major types: (1) surface treatment of the diamond: metallization and roughening of the diamond surface; (2) modification of metal matrix: the addition of strong carbide forming elements, rare earth elements and some non-metallic elements, and pre-alloying or refining of matrix powders; (3) change in preparation technology: the adjustment of the sintering process and the application of new technologies. Additionally, the methods used in the evaluation of diamond retention strength are introduced, including three categories: (1) instrument detection methods: scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffractometry, energy dispersive spectrometry and Raman spectroscopy; (2) mechanical test methods: bending strength analytical method, tension ring test method, and other test methods for chemical bonding strength; (3) mechanical calculation methods: theoretical calculation and numerical computation. Finally, future research directions are discussed.

The excerpt indicates that freshly prepared aluminum develops a thin native/amorphous oxide in air or dry oxygen at room temperature, typically about 10–20 Å (1–2 nm). In the reported experiment, oxidation in oxygen at room temperature for 5 hours produced an approximately 15 Å oxide. Humid air accelerates subsequent surface transformation: pure aluminum preoxidized at room temperature increased from 15 Å to 22 Å after one week at 80% relative humidity, whereas the corresponding increase in dry atmosphere was only 1 Å. The authors attribute the humid-atmosphere growth primarily to hydration of Al2O3, producing aluminum hydroxide; under the study conditions, hydroxide formation was detectable after exposure periods of one day to one week. For technically pure alloy, humidity caused localized corrosion and hydroxide formation around Fe- and Si-containing noble precipitates such as Al3Fe and α-AlFeSi. The excerpt does not provide a direct quantitative assessment of how a 1–2 nm oxide/hydroxide layer affects SEM-EDS measurements at 5–15 kV. It only states that hydroxide particles could be observed by SEM because Al2O3 has a higher secondary-electron yield than Al(OH)3. Thus, the passage supports the formation rate and approximate native thickness, but not a definitive claim about EDS accuracy or correction requirements.

The hydration reaction is reported to proceed rapidly initially and then slow substantially: the oxide reaches its maximum measured thickness after one week, with no further increase after one month. Water exposure can also produce Al(OH)3, particularly on technically pure aluminum alloy particles or corrosion-active intermetallic regions; the hydroxide decomposes under UHV analysis conditions and during ion etching. ## pqac-00000049

From text 'zhao2018areviewof pages 1-3'.

Xiaojun Zhao and Longchen Duan. A review of the diamond retention capacity of metal bond matrices. ArXiv, 8:307, Apr 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met8050307, doi:10.3390/met8050307. This article has 91 citations.

The excerpt characterizes diamond as relatively chemically inert toward metal matrices, with a high interfacial energy at metal–diamond surfaces. Consequently, chemical reactions or wetting/infiltration by metals are difficult rather than spontaneous. The article distinguishes chemical bonding from mechanical retention: chemical bonding can arise at the diamond–metal interface under the elevated pressure and temperature conditions of sintering, and its occurrence depends on metal composition, particle characteristics, atmosphere, and sintering temperature and duration. In the absence of chemical reaction or diffusion, diamond is retained primarily by mechanical interlocking. The excerpt also identifies three possible metal–diamond interfacial behaviors: diamond degradation and graphite formation, carbide formation that can produce strong bonding, and inert behavior involving only mechanical bonding. It therefore supports the conclusion that room-temperature chemical bonding between diamond and aluminum or other metals cannot be established from this passage; the discussion concerns reactions under processing conditions, especially sintering. The excerpt does not provide information about the surface termination chemistry of nanodiamond particles, such as whether they are terminated with hydrogen, oxygen, hydroxyl, or other groups.

## pqac-00000050

From text 'sumant2007surfacechemistryand pages 1-2'.

A. V. Sumant, D. S. Grierson, J. E. Gerbi, J. A. Carlisle, O. Auciello, and R. W. Carpick. Surface chemistry and bonding configuration of ultrananocrystalline diamond surfaces and their effects on nanotribological properties. Physical Review B, 76:235429, Dec 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevb.76.235429, doi:10.1103/physrevb.76.235429. This article has 146 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that diamond surfaces are not universally or intrinsically chemically inert; their reactivity depends strongly on surface preparation, bonding configuration, and termination. For UNCD, the as-etched underside contains a higher sp2 fraction and some oxidized carbon, showing that oxygen-containing surface chemistry can be present. Atomic-hydrogen exposure removes reactive carbon groups, polar groups such as C=O, and pi-bonded C=C groups, replacing them with fully saturated hydrogen-terminated bonds. This produces an effectively inert surface with minimal interaction with a contacting counterface: the reported work of adhesion falls from 59.2±2 mJ/m2 for the untreated underside to 10.2±0.4 mJ/m2 after hydrogen exposure, near the van der Waals-interaction level, with friction also substantially reduced. The excerpt does not establish whether diamond forms chemical bonds with aluminum or other metals at room temperature; it only reports low adhesion against a diamond nanotip and prior low adhesion/friction against tungsten-carbide tips. It also does not provide a general surface-termination analysis for nanodiamond particles. It supports hydrogen termination for hydrogen-treated diamond and oxidized carbon for the as-etched UNCD underside, but cannot determine whether a particular nanodiamond sample is predominantly hydrogen-, oxygen-, or hydroxyl-terminated.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevb.76.235429, doi:10.1103/physrevb.76.235429. This article has 146 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns the surface chemistry and tribological behavior of ultrananocrystalline diamond (UNCD), rather than bulk diamond or direct reactions with aluminum and other metals. It demonstrates that UNCD surfaces can have different chemical states depending on processing and orientation: the study compares the topside, an as-etched underside, and a hydrogen-terminated underside. Hydrogen-plasma treatment was performed specifically so that atomic hydrogen would saturate dangling bonds on the newly exposed surface. The authors also quantify the fraction of carbon in sp2 bonding configurations, indicating that UNCD surfaces and interfaces can contain non-diamond carbon rather than being chemically uniform or perfectly inert. The films were fabricated using mechanical polishing and ultrasonic nanodiamond seeding, and the substrate was removed with an HF:HNO3 bath to expose the underside. The excerpt does not report experiments on aluminum, metal bonding, or room-temperature chemical reactions between diamond and metals. It also does not characterize oxygen- or hydroxyl-terminated nanodiamond particles directly; its explicit surface functionalization discussed here is hydrogen termination. XANES, XPS, and AES were used or planned to characterize surface composition, but the provided passage contains no resulting oxygen, hydroxyl, or metal-bonding data.

The excerpt indicates that ultrananocrystalline diamond (UNCD) surfaces are not chemically featureless or necessarily inert. Before hydrogen-plasma treatment, XPS detects oxygen on both the exposed topside and the nucleation underside, with a somewhat greater oxygen concentration on the underside (approximately 12–15 atomic percent versus 8–10 atomic percent on the topside). The underside also contains a carbon component assigned to sp2-hybridized carbon, such as graphite or amorphous carbon, although the excerpt notes that quantitatively determining carbon hybridization by XPS is controversial. Atomic hydrogen treatment changes the surface: it etches nondiamond phases much more rapidly than pure diamond and removes small contaminant particles, producing a smoother surface. These observations show that UNCD surface chemistry depends on processing, nucleation method, and post-treatment, and can include oxygen-containing species, nondiamond carbon, and hydrogen-reactive contaminants. The excerpt does not directly discuss aluminum or other metal adhesion, chemical-bond formation at room temperature, or identify whether oxygen is present specifically as hydroxyl, carbonyl, ether, or other functional groups. It also does not establish a general rule for hydrogen termination of all nanodiamond particles; it only discusses hydrogen-plasma exposure and its effects on UNCD surfaces.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevb.76.235429, doi:10.1103/physrevb.76.235429. This article has 146 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that diamond surfaces are not inherently described as chemically inert under all preparation conditions. The acid-etched underside of ultrananocrystalline diamond (UNCD) is predominantly sp3-bonded but contains higher fractions of nondiamond phases, including amorphous and oxidized carbon, than the as-grown topside. Hydrogen-plasma treatment removes contaminants, including polar oxide groups, saturates dangling bonds, and produces an inert, hydrogen-terminated surface. This termination substantially lowers adhesion and friction, with the exposed UNCD described as hydrogen-terminated after treatment. The excerpt does not discuss whether diamond forms chemical bonds with aluminum or other metals at room temperature, so it cannot establish the presence or absence of metal–diamond bonding. It also does not characterize nanodiamond particles specifically or determine whether their surfaces are terminated by hydrogen, oxygen, or hydroxyl groups. Its findings apply primarily to UNCD film surfaces and show that surface chemistry depends strongly on growth, etching, contamination, oxidation, and hydrogen-plasma treatment. Thus, the passage supports hydrogen termination and possible oxidized surface species under particular processing conditions, but provides no direct evidence about aluminum bonding or the relative prevalence of hydrogen, oxygen, and hydroxyl termination on nanodiamond particles.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevb.76.235429, doi:10.1103/physrevb.76.235429. This article has 146 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not establish that diamond is universally chemically inert, nor does it discuss whether diamond forms bonds with aluminum or other metals at room temperature. It instead shows that diamond surface chemistry depends strongly on preparation, crystallinity, and termination. TEY XANES measurements probe the near-surface region and distinguish sp3 diamond bonding from sp2 carbon and oxygen-containing species. The as-etched underside of ultrananocrystalline diamond (UNCD) contains more amorphous/sp2 carbon than the topside, along with evidence for chemisorbed oxygen and carboxyl groups. Hydrogen-plasma treatment substantially reduces the sp2/amorphous-carbon signal, removes chemically bonded oxygen, and produces a hydrogen-terminated surface with stronger diamond character. A C–H resonance is observed, while the C=O-related feature disappears after treatment. Thus, the excerpt supports hydrogen termination for appropriately treated UNCD surfaces, while untreated surfaces can contain oxygenated groups and nondiamond carbon. It provides no direct information about aluminum–diamond or other metal–diamond chemical bonding at room temperature, and it does not characterize the surface termination of free nanodiamond particles specifically. Such conclusions would require separate measurements accounting for particle synthesis, oxidation, purification, and storage conditions.

## pqac-00000055

From text 'zhao2018areviewof pages 3-5'.

Xiaojun Zhao and Longchen Duan. A review of the diamond retention capacity of metal bond matrices. ArXiv, 8:307, Apr 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met8050307, doi:10.3390/met8050307. This article has 91 citations.

The excerpt distinguishes between chemically reactive and inert diamond–metal interfaces. Diamond retention can be purely mechanical when no chemical reaction or diffusion occurs, which the review calls “inert behavior.” Chemical bonding is described primarily for strong carbide-forming metals or elements such as Mo, Ti, V, W, and Cr, and it requires suitable processing conditions, typically heat treatment or sintering. These elements can generate an interfacial carbide layer that bonds to the diamond and also joins to the metal matrix. The excerpt therefore supports the conclusion that diamond is not universally chemically inert, but its direct chemical interaction with metals depends strongly on the metal chemistry and processing temperature. It does not provide evidence about whether diamond forms chemical bonds with aluminum specifically at room temperature; in fact, the mechanisms discussed are high-temperature carbide formation, diffusion, and sintering rather than ambient-temperature reactions. The excerpt also does not discuss the surface chemistry or terminal groups of nanodiamond particles. It gives no information to determine whether nanodiamond surfaces are predominantly hydrogen-, oxygen-, or hydroxyl-terminated. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Aspect | Colloidal silica final polish | 0.1 µm water-based polycrystalline diamond suspension |
|---|---|---|
| **Abrasive and carrier** | Nanoscale amorphous SiO₂ in a usually alkaline aqueous sol; metallographic products commonly operate near pH 9.5–10 (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000031) | Discrete diamond particles in water with small amounts of PEG and surfactant; the specified PACE WPC-0110 contains no silica or alumina |
| **Behavior during drying** | Evaporation concentrates particles and ions. Surface silanols condense into Si–O–Si bridges, particles aggregate into a three-dimensional gel, and capillary drying shrinks and densifies the deposit. Evaporation can produce hard, crystallized or agglomerated residue (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000024) | Water evaporates, leaving loose or agglomerated diamond plus traces of PEG and surfactant. Diamond does **not** undergo silica-type hydrolysis, silanol condensation, or sol–gel network formation |
| **Possible bonding to aluminum** | Nanoparticles have high surface area and abundant silanols. Hydrogen bonding, mechanical anchoring, and possible condensation with hydroxylated native alumina to form interfacial Si–O–Al linkages can strengthen adhesion. Direct evidence quantifying Si–O–Al bonding during metallographic polishing is limited; the general silica-network mechanism is well established (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | At ambient polishing conditions, diamond is relatively inert toward metals. Strong diamond–metal chemical bonding generally requires elevated-temperature processing and carbide-forming elements; ordinary polishing residue should be retained primarily by adsorption, capillary deposition, or mechanical trapping (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000055) |
| **Likely dried residue** | A silica-rich gel or xerogel or hard particulate film, potentially containing alkali ions and polishing additives; commonly appears as a white haze or adherent layer (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000035) | Diamond particles, traces of water-soluble PEG, surfactant, and ordinary polishing swarf. Diamond surfaces may contain oxygenated or other termination groups, but these do not create a silica-like gel network (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052) |
| **Ease of removal after drying** | Often difficult. Hardened residue may require detergent and gentle cotton swabbing or repolishing; dried silica on the cloth can become extremely difficult to remove and cause scratching (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000035) | Expected to be substantially easier: prompt water rinsing should remove most carrier, PEG, surfactant, and suspended diamond. A dried deposit may require detergent and gentle swabbing or brief ultrasonics, especially where particles lodge in pores or the mount/specimen gap. Direct comparative studies on dried diamond suspension on aluminum were not found |
| **Need for continuous alcohol spraying during transfer** | Keeping the face wet and cleaning immediately is justified because evaporation rapidly concentrates the sol and promotes adherent silica deposition. Alcohol is useful for water displacement, but flushing with water before drying is central (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000024) | **No silica-style continuous methanol spray is chemically required.** Do not deliberately allow the slurry to dry, but ordinary prompt transfer to a water rinse is sufficient. A brief delay is less consequential than with colloidal silica |
| **EDS contamination risk** | High and directly relevant: residual SiO₂ adds Si and O and can attenuate substrate X-rays, with greater relative influence at lower accelerating voltage. Polishing-induced surface films and contaminants can bias quantitative X-ray microanalysis (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000034) | No false Si or Al contribution from the stated suspension. Remaining diamond or organics can contribute carbon, attenuate low-energy X-rays, obscure small features, and trap swarf; carbon may also be difficult to distinguish from phenolic-mount or carbon-coating contributions |
| **Recommended immediate cleaning** | Before removal, stop silica delivery and flush with water where the equipment allows. Then rinse promptly with running or deionized water; use dilute neutral detergent and gentle cotton swabbing if haze remains; rinse thoroughly; displace water with ethanol or IPA; dry immediately with clean warm air or nitrogen (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000024) | Rinse promptly and generously with deionized water while gently swabbing with clean soft cotton or a lint-free applicator. If needed, use dilute neutral laboratory detergent, followed by a complete DI-water rinse. Finish with clean ethanol or IPA and dry immediately with nitrogen or clean warm air |
| **Ultrasonic cleaning** | Brief ultrasonics can remove residual particles, but prolonged treatment may drive slurry into mount gaps, dislodge weak phases, or attack poorly impregnated LPBF porosity (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019) | Optional rather than routine: approximately 30–120 seconds in clean DI water with a trace of neutral detergent, followed by fresh DI water and then ethanol or IPA, is a reasonable validation starting point. Avoid long cycles because AlSi10Mg pores, Si particles, and phenolic-mount gaps may retain liquid or debris; no manufacturer consensus time specific to this suspension was found |
| **Methanol versus ethanol or IPA** | Methanol is not uniquely required. Ethanol is explicitly recommended for water displacement and final rinsing; IPA is also used for ultrasonic cleaning. Solvent purity, complete rinsing, rapid evaporation, and residue control matter more than selecting methanol specifically (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000024) | Ethanol or IPA is suitable and generally preferable to methanol on toxicity grounds. Alcohol is a final water-displacement and drying aid—not the primary cleaner for water-soluble PEG, surfactant, particles, or ionic residue |
| **Practical cleaning urgency** | **Seconds to immediate:** prevent visible drying before the water flush | **Prompt but not frantic:** aim to begin the water rinse within roughly a minute and never let a thick slurry puddle dry; continuous spraying throughout transfer is unnecessary |
| **Recommended verification for quantitative SEM-EDS** | Inspect at low kV for haze or particles and compare Si/O on a cleaned specimen with a freshly repolished control. Residue effects can be stronger at 5 kV than at 15 kV because the sampled volume is shallower (pqac-00000022) | Establish the procedure experimentally using paired specimens: immediate rinse versus deliberately dried residue, then map C/O/Si at 5 and 15 kV. This is important because direct published evidence for PEG, surfactant, or diamond residue from WPC-0110 on AlSi10Mg was not found |

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We final-polish phenolic (Bakelite)-mounted, as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg on a Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher for quantitative SEM-EDS (5-15 kV). Until now the final step was 0.05 um colloidal silica for about 4-5 hours. When the puck came out of the bowl, the operator had to keep spraying the face with methanol, continuously, until it was cleaned, because colloidal silica left on the face starts drying, gelling and crystallizing within seconds of air exposure, bonds to the surface and is then very hard to remove; residual silica also adds Si to the EDS result. We are replacing colloidal silica with a water-based polycrystalline diamond suspension, 0.1 um (PACE Technologies DIAMAT WPC-0110: about 94-98% water, diamond, <=0.1% polyethylene glycol, <=0.2% surfactant; the vendor confirms no silica or alumina), on a low-nap synthetic polishing cloth with adhesive backing.
Questions:
(1) Does a 0.1 um water-based diamond suspension require the same keep-it-wet, continuous alcohol (methanol) spray handling when the specimen is removed, as colloidal silica does? Explain the mechanism that makes colloidal silica dry, gel and bond to a polished surface (sol-gel condensation, pH, Si-O-metal bonding, particle size and surface area) and whether a diamond suspension shares any of it. What residue, if any, does a dried water-based diamond suspension leave on aluminum (diamond particles, PEG or surfactant films), and how hard is it to remove compared with dried colloidal silica?
(2) What cleaning sequence after the final diamond step do the literature and manufacturers (Buehler, Struers, PACE, Allied, QATM/ATM) recommend for aluminum alloys: water rinse, detergent or soap, swabbing, ethanol or methanol or isopropanol rinse, ultrasonic time, drying with warm air or nitrogen? Is methanol specifically needed, or is ethanol or isopropanol equivalent?
(3) Does the water in the suspension, or a delay before cleaning, cause staining, pitting, hydroxide or oxide growth on Al-Si alloys that would change quantitative EDS (O, Al, Si, Mg), and how quickly?
Cite primary literature and manufacturer application notes where possible, and say clearly where evidence is missing.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address these three detailed questions about metallographic polishing of AlSi10Mg with diamond suspension vs. colloidal silica.

Abstract:
Liquid metal reaction media provides exciting new avenues for synthesizing low‐dimensional materials. Here, the synthesis of atomically thin sheets and nanofibers of boehmite (γ‐AlOOH) and their transformation into cubic alumina (γ‐Al2O3) via annealing is explored. The sheets are as thin as one orthorhombic boehmite unit cell. The addition of aluminum into a room temperature alloy of gallium, followed by exposing the melt to either liquid water or water vapor, allows growing either 2D sheets or 1D fibers, respectively. The isolated oxide hydroxides feature large surface areas, with the sheet morphologies also showing a high Young's modulus. The method is green, since the liquid metal solvent can be fully reused. The ultrathin boehmite sheets are found suitable for the development of freestanding membrane filters that enable excellent separation of heavy metal ions and oil from aqueous solutions at extraordinary filtrate flux. The developed liquid metal‐based synthesis process offers a sustainable, green, and rapid method for synthesizing nanomorphologies of metal oxides which are challenging to obtain by conventional methods. The process is both sustainable and scalable and may be explored for the creation of other types of metal oxide compounds.

growing use of duplex stainless steels (DSSs) has spurred extensive research and development, particularly concerning weldability challenges. The increasing interest in additive manufacturing (AM) using directed energy deposition (DED) has further highlighted the need for precise sample preparation to ensure accurate microstructural characterization. This paper consolidates best practices for preparing samples to effectively reveal microstructures and secondary phases in DSSs. By optimizing polishing techniques and etching methods, the work provides guidelines for distinguishing ferrite and austenite across the base material, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and weld metal, while also enabling the detection of intermetallic phases and discrete secondary precipitates. Examples of typical deviations, etching phenomena, and potential pitfalls are also provided. The preparation strategies presented are tailored to support subsequent analysis using light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Azizur", title = "Synthesis and Microstructural Characterization of Ti/SiO2 Composite Powder Fabricated by Powder Metallurgy", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Jul", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10034168/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10034168/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Titanium/Silicon dioxide (Ti/SiO 2 ) composite powder was prepared through powder metallurgy process of high-energy mechanical mixing, uniaxial compaction under 200 MPa and vacuum sintering under 1100 °C for 4 h. Multi-technique characterization of phase composition, chemical bonding and microstructure was done by using the X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDX). XRD unambiguously confirmed retention of the α-quartz SiO 2 phase (ICDD 00-033-1161), with the principal (101) reflection at 2θ = 26.661° yielding d101 = 3.342 Å and hexagonal lattice parameters a = 4.913 Å, c = 5.405 Å. The crystallite size obtained from Scherrer analysis was 138 ± 10 nm, a nanoscale value corresponding to nanograin refinement. FTIR spectroscopy revealed the Si–O–Si asymmetric stretching band at 1010 cm -1 , the presence of surface silanol groups at 3512–3657 cm -1 , and the presence of Ti–O vibrational modes in the region of 528–663 cm -1 . Most importantly, the co-presence of Ti–O–Si mixed-bonding signatures yield spectroscopic evidence for chemical interaction at the Ti/SiO 2 interface, other than mechanical mixing. SEM/EDX analysis showed the distribution of elements and microstructural features of the composite, which was in agreement with the compositional targets. Thermodynamic stability of the composite is verified by the absence of secondary phases of TiSi₂ and TiO 2 in the XRD. These results provide a clear relationship between structure, processing, and properties of Ti/SiO 2 composites for applications such as aerospace, biomedical, and catalytic uses.

Welding diagrams, taking into account composition and process parameters, could not generally account for the experimental observations of non-cracked versus cracked AM 316L samples. EBSD phase maps in all three AM samples exhibited a fully austenitic microstructure not only in the bulk sample but also near-surface. Analysis of microcracked regions in the AM samples showed the presence of local enrichment of Ni, Cu and P. Automated SEM/EDS analysis on feedstock powder samples prepared for cross-section examination revealed a fine, foreign particulate contaminant, expected to arise from NiCrCuP alloy cross-contamination during atomization, to be completely embedded in a 316L powder particle. This type of contamination would not have been revealed on examination of powder mounted onto a SEM stub, a common approach to assess powder quality. Based on this analysis, it is recommended to consider including automated SEM/EDS analysis on powder cross-sections in any standardization protocol for quality control of powders, to increase the chances of detection and identification of fine cross-contaminants. It is also recommended that atomization of NiCrCuP alloy should no longer precede atomization of 316L alloy. Environmentally friendly synthesis of silicon dioxide nanoparticles and their application for the removal of emerging contaminants in aqueous media Valid Text Names: 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 1-3', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 3-5', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 5-7', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 7-9', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 9-10', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 10-12', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 12-14', 'tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis pages 14-16' BibTex: @article{tejedor2022environmentallyfriendlysynthesis, author = "Tejedor, Jennifer and Guerrero, Victor H. and Vizuete, Karla and Debut, Alexis", title = "Environmentally friendly synthesis of silicon dioxide nanoparticles and their application for the removal of emerging contaminants in aqueous media", year = "2022", journal = "Journal of Physics: Conference Series", volume = "2238", pages = "012005", month = "Apr", doi = "10.1088/1742-6596/2238/1/012005", url = "https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/2238/1/012005", publisher = "IOP Publishing", issue = "1", issn = "1742-6588" } Abstract: The highly detrimental potential effects that emerging contaminants have for the environment and human health demand the development of sustainable technologies to eliminate these pollutants. In this work, an eco-friendly approach was followed to synthesize S1O2 nanoparticles to be used to remove caffeine and triclosan from synthetic waters. Rice husk was the precursor used, which was subjected to acid leaching treatments using acetic and oxalic acids, and pyrolysis for 2 h at 700 °C. The resulting powders were characterized by X-ray diffraction, Raman and infrared spectroscopies, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller method, and scanning and transmission electron microscopy. The particles synthesized were amorphous, had an average size between 4.6 and 9.6 nm, and specific surface areas between 208 and 223 m2/g. The adsorptive performance of the nanosilica obtained using acetic acid was studied by batch tests. The optimum dosage, maximum removal efficiencies and maximum adsorption capacities were 8 g/L, 76%, and 2.74 mg/g, and 24 g/L, 48%, and 0.75 mg/g for triclosan and caffeine, respectively. Abstract:
Abstract Silica nanoparticles (SNPs), one of the most widely researched materials in modern science, are now commonly exploited in surface coatings, biomedicine, catalysis, and engineering of novel self‐assembling materials. Theoretical approaches are invaluable to enhancing fundamental understanding of SNP properties and behavior. Tremendous research attention is dedicated to modeling silica structure, the silica‐water interface, and functionalization of silica surfaces for tailored applications. In this review, the range of theoretical methodologies are discussed that have been employed to model bare silica and functionalized silica. The evolution of silica modeling approaches is detailed, including classical, quantum mechanical, and hybrid methods and highlight in particular the last decade of theoretical simulation advances. It is started with discussing investigations of bare silica systems, focusing on the fundamental interactions at the silica‐water interface, following with a comprehensively review of the modeling studies that examine the interaction of silica with functional ligands, peptides, ions, surfactants, polymers, and carbonaceous species. The review is concluded with the perspective on existing challenges in the field and promising future directions that will further enhance the utility and importance of the theoretical approaches in guiding the rational design of SNPs for applications in engineering and biomedicine.

Abstract:
An attempt was made to control the surface charge of colloidal silica nanoparticles with 20 nm and 100 nm diameters. Untreated silica nanoparticles were determined to be highly negatively charged and have stable hydrodynamic sizes in a wide pH range. To change the surface to a positively charged form, various coating agents, such as amine containing molecules, multivalent metal cation, or amino acids, were used to treat the colloidal silica nanoparticles. Molecules with chelating amine sites were determined to have high affinity with the silica surface to make agglomerations or gel-like networks. Amino acid coatings resulted in relatively stable silica colloids with a modified surface charge. Three amino acid moiety coatings (L-serine, L-histidine, and L-arginine) exhibited surface charge modifying efficacy of L-histidine > L-arginine > L-serine and hydrodynamic size preservation efficacy of L-serine > L-arginine > L-histidine. The time dependent change in L-arginine coated colloidal silica was investigated by measuring the pattern of the backscattered light in a Turbiscan™. The results indicated that both the 20 nm and 100 nm L-arginine coated silica samples were fairly stable in terms of colloidal homogeneity, showing only slight coalescence and sedimentation.

## 3. Unravelling the Chemical Influence of Water on the PMMA/Aluminum Oxide Hybrid Interface In Situ

Abstract:
Understanding the stability of chemical interactions at the polymer/metal oxide interface under humid conditions is vital to understand the long-term durability of hybrid systems. Therefore, the interface of ultrathin PMMA films on native aluminum oxide, deposited by reactive adsorption, was studied. The characterization of the interface of the coated substrates was performed using ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (APXPS), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy in the Kretschmann geometry (ATR-FTIR Kretschmann) and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS). The formation of hydrogen bonds and carboxylate ionic bonds at the interface are observed. The formed ionic bond is stable up to 5 Torr water vapour pressure as shown by APXPS. However, when the coated samples are exposed to an excess of aqueous electrolyte, an increase in the amount of carboxylate bonds at the interface, as a result of hydrolysis of the methoxy group, is observed by ATR-FTIR Kretschmann. These observations, supported by ToF-SIMS spectra, lead to the proposal of an adsorption mechanism of PMMA on aluminum oxide, which shows the formation of methanol at the interface and the effect of water molecules on the different interfacial interactions.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) and post-CMP cleaning are critical steps in the current semiconductor manufacturing process. These processes require ensuring atomic-scale flatness and complete removal of contaminants. This review examines the use of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the atomic-scale mechanisms underlying CMP and postcleaning, focusing on four major MD methodologies: classical MD, reactive force field MD (ReaxFF), tight-binding quantum chemical MD (TB-QC MD), and ab initio MD (AIMD). Classical MD provides a foundation for simulating large-scale systems but lacks accuracy for modeling chemical reactions. ReaxFF allows real-time bond breaking and formation simulations during CMP. TB-QC MD combines quantum accuracy with classical efficiency, enabling exploration of the effects of chemical reactions on friction and material removal. AIMD directly calculates atomic interactions for precise depictions of chemical processes, although it is computationally expensive. MD simulations act as a “computational microscope”, enhancing CMP and postcleaning processes by quantifying interactions, material removal pathways, and contaminant desorption. Future research should address multiscale modeling challenges, improve AIMD efficiency, and develop accurate potential functions to propel semiconductor manufacturing toward greater precision and efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
The functional surfactants, as the additional additives in the standard glycol-based lubricant were studied and optimized to reduce and protect the surface of the magnetic read/write head from deposited contaminants during the lapping processes. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) results identified that the black contamination was bismuth (Bi) particles, came out from lapping plate during the lapping process due to wear. Selected surfactants exhibited the results in reduce and prevent the deposition of contaminants by forming the micelle beyond their critical micelle concentration (CMC) values. We found that both polyethoxylate alcohol (PEAL) and quaternary amines (QA) can form their micelle in glycol-based lubricant at the ratio of 1 %wt. Polyoxyethylene sorbitan monolaurate (PO) can protect the surface by its oxyethylene groups group at the 0.2 %wt in based lubricant. The characteristics and performances of modified lubricants were measured the change in magnetoresistive resistance value (%DMRR) from quasi-static test (QST). The modified lubricants had minor distribution failure of slider lower than standard lubricant. Moreover, the potentiodynamic polarization?measurement results indicated that additional surfactant can also yield almost 300% better performances than the standard lubricant in term of corrosion protection during lapping processes. Thus, these surfactants can function both as the contamination protective additive and as anti-corrosion additive. These modified lubricants can also keep the lap time and other physical performances to match the fabrication requirements.

The excerpt describes drying and gelation as a progressive sol-gel network-forming process. Water hydrolyzes alkoxy groups to produce silanol (Si-OH) groups; silanol condensation then creates siloxane (Si-O-Si) bonds while releasing water or alcohol. Continued condensation causes molecules and particles to aggregate into a continuous gel network. During drying, water and alcohol leave the network, causing shrinkage and reinforcing the gel. pH, water-to-silicon ratio, reagent concentration, temperature, ageing, and drying govern hydrolysis, condensation, particle formation, and final structure. At pH above 7, silica is more soluble and particles can grow; under specified alkaline conditions, spherical nanoparticles form, while higher temperatures produce larger particles. These factors imply that particle size and available surface area affect aggregation, network formation, drying shrinkage, and the extent of contact with a substrate. The excerpt documents strong adhesion of sol-gel films to silicon, silicon dioxide, and aluminum surfaces, but it does not explicitly describe Si-O-metal bond formation at polished metal surfaces. Thus, specific chemical bonding to metal, or a detailed role for surface area in metal adhesion, is not directly established in this passage; it only provides the broader silica condensation, particle-growth, drying, and adhesion framework.

The excerpt describes colloidal silica gelation as the formation of a three-dimensional network when condensed colloidal clusters crosslink and entrap the liquid. Silanol hydrolysis and subsequent silanol condensation/oxolation govern this process. At low pH, condensation is relatively slow and Si–O–Si chain growth, branching, and later crosslinking produce a polymeric, relatively low-pore-volume and microporous gel. Under basic conditions, hydrolyzed species are rapidly consumed, producing larger agglomerates that crosslink into a particulate gel with higher pore volume and mesoporosity. pH therefore controls both reaction rates and network architecture. During aging and drying, polycondensation creates additional chemical bonds, while syneresis expels liquid and causes shrinkage; coarsening can enlarge particle necks and fill smaller pores, reducing microporosity and surface area. The excerpt notes that silica’s partly covalent Si–O bonding permits flexible Si–O–Si angles and relatively open networks. It does not directly explain bonding to polished metal surfaces or explicitly discuss Si–O–metal bonds, particle-size optimization, or the detailed drying mechanism at a metal interface. It does, however, provide the relevant general framework: surface hydroxyl chemistry, condensation, colloidal-cluster size, pore structure, aging, and evolving surface area would be expected to influence adhesion and drying.

Acid and base catalysis produce different structures: under acidic conditions hydrolysis is faster than condensation, giving a weakly branched gel; under basic conditions condensation dominates, producing a more highly branched gel. The hydrolysis rate has a minimum near pH 7, and pH, temperature, water-to-alkoxide ratio, and the organic substituent structure affect the process. The text also notes that silicate activation is pH-dependent and that acidification can convert silicate anions into tetrahedrally coordinated precursors capable of oxolation. Drying removes water and/or alcohol, causing the gel to shrink while it remains flexible. Continued drying increases cross-linking and stiffness; once the gel can no longer shrink, liquid recedes into the pores and capillary stresses develop at curved menisci, potentially producing cracks. Condensation reactions link silanol-containing species through Si-O-Si bonds and may generate either alcohol or water. pH strongly affects both hydrolysis and condensation: silica has its longest gel times near its isoelectric point, approximately pH 2.2, while reaction rates increase under more acidic or more basic conditions. Acid catalysis initially favors formation of a relatively open network, whereas base catalysis promotes highly cross-linked, larger sol particles that form gels with larger pores. Abstract:
This experimental work is aimed at studying the effect of microstructural modifications induced by post-processing heat treatments on the corrosion behavior of silicon-aluminum alloys produced by means of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The manufacturing technique leads to microstructures characterized by the presence of melt pools, which are quite different compared to casting alloys. In this study, the behavior of an AlSi10Mg alloy was evaluated by means of intergranular corrosion tests according to ISO 11846 standard on heat-treated samples ranging from 200 to 500 °C as well as on untreated samples. We found that temperatures above 200 °C reduced microhardness of the alloy, and different corrosion morphologies occurred due to the modification of both size and distribution of silicon precipitates. Selective penetrating attacks occurred at melt pool borders. The intergranular corrosion phenomena were less intense for as-produced specimens without heat treatments compared to the heat-treated specimens at 200 and 300 °C. General corrosion morphologies were noticed for specimens heat treated at temperatures exceeding 400 °C.

Abstract:
In this work, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) process was applied on AlSi10Mg samples, produced with laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), in the as printed condition and after different heat treatments, and, for comparison, on as-cast samples of AlSi10Mg. PEO process was performed in direct-current mode using high current densities and short time in a basic silicate electrolyte. The not-uniform silicon distribution produced a not-homogenous distribution of silicon into the coatings. The particular cellular structure of the as printed sample induced the formation of a coating with a higher amorphous fraction, in comparison with the ones produced on the other samples. The higher thickness and lower porosity of the coatings obtained on the annealed and as printed samples resulted in an increase of the corrosion resistance.
